content.intro: This lesson introduces understanding the staging area as part of Basic Git Workflow. It follows the supplied Git curriculum and adds an original explanation, an inspectable command example, troubleshooting notes, and a practice task.
content.why_it_matters: The index is a deliberate staging area between edited files and the next commit. It allows a commit to include selected hunks from a larger working-tree change rather than forcing every modification into one snapshot.

content_blocks.title: Working tree to commit: staging lifecycle
content_blocks.alt_text: Edits begin in the working tree, selected changes enter the index with git add, and git commit records the index as a repository snapshot.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** The index is a deliberate staging area between edited files and the next commit. It allows a commit to include selected hunks from a larger working-tree change rather than forcing every modification into one snapshot.

For **Understanding the Staging Area**, keep the named subtopics in view: Why staging is separate from committing; Reviewing staged changes; Staging selected modifications; Repeatedly updating the index. Treat those as the scope of this lesson, then practise the smallest workflow that demonstrates the idea.

content_blocks.title: How to reason about it
content_blocks.text: **Before you run a command:** decide what state you are inspecting or changing, identify whether the effect is local or remote, and write down what evidence would count as success. Run from inside a repository after staging one or more paths. The command does not change files.

content_blocks.title: Safety and verification checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Start with git status --short --branch. For destructive or history-rewriting operations, review the exact target, create a recovery reference when appropriate, and keep valuable work backed up. Never put credentials, access tokens or private keys in course submissions.

common_mistakes.problem: Running a state-changing command without confirming the target repository or branch.
common_mistakes.why: A command may affect the wrong working tree or move a reference that other work depends on.
common_mistakes.fix: Check git rev-parse --show-toplevel and git status --short --branch before proceeding.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a command succeeded because no error was visible.
common_mistakes.why: Some Git commands are silent on success, and some expected actions are blocked by repository state or permissions.
common_mistakes.fix: Verify status, log, references, remote state or the named output explicitly.

common_mistakes.problem: Using an example placeholder literally or applying a destructive example to valuable work.
common_mistakes.why: Paths, branch names and object IDs depend on the current repository; restore/reset/clean operations can discard work.
common_mistakes.fix: Substitute real practice values, use a disposable repository, and preview changes before proceeding.
